modern_osis:
Ezekiel — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)

Ezekiel was a priest who was taken captive to Chaldea with Jehoiachin.

Henry believes all Ezekiel's prophecies were delivered there, at a place north of Babylon.

Their chief purpose was to comfort the prophet's fellow exiles.

Ezekiel was called to warn of terrible disasters coming upon Judah, especially judgment against false prophets, as well as against neighboring nations.

He also announced the future restoration of Israel and Judah from their places of dispersion and their blessed condition in later days under the Messiah.

Much teaching about Christ appears in this book, particularly toward its end.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesEzekiel's vision of God, and of the angelic host.1–14The conduct of Divine Providence.15–25A revelation of the Son of man upon his heavenly throne.26–28
Ezekiel sees the living creatures (verses 1–14)

It is a mercy when God's word reaches us in the midst of affliction, and our duty to listen to it diligently.

God's voice came through the Holy Spirit, in abundant light and power.

The visions seem intended to fill Ezekiel's mind with great and exalted thoughts of God.

They would awaken fear in sinners while comforting those who feared God and humbled themselves.

The first part, in verses 4–14, pictures God attended by a vast company of angels—his messengers and servants, who do his will.

The scene inspires solemn awe of his holiness and displeasure against sin, yet also hope for blessings.

The fire is surrounded by glory.

Although we cannot discover everything about God by searching, we can see the brightness surrounding his glory.

The living creatures came from the fire, reminding us that angels receive their being and strength from God.

Their appearances combine outstanding qualities.

A human being has understanding, and the angels understand far more.

A lion represents strength and boldness.

An ox represents diligence, patience and tireless work.

An eagle represents speed, sharp vision and soaring height.

The angels surpass human beings in all these qualities.

They have wings, showing the speed with which they carry out God's commands.

They stand upright, firm and steady.

But they have hands as well as wings.

Some people rush from place to place but never accomplish useful work. They have wings without hands.

God's servants, however, are ready both to go and to act.

They move straight ahead, not turning aside to waste time on trivial matters.

Their work needs no correction because they follow the Spirit's direction.

Their fiery appearance suggests seraphim, or burning ones, representing their ardent love for God and zeal in serving him.

Even visions we cannot fully understand can teach useful lessons.

We should attend especially to whatever concerns our peace and duty, leaving secret matters to the Lord.

The wheels picture God's Providence (verses 15–25)

The wheels represent the changing events of Providence.

A wheel turns: first one spoke is above, then another. Yet the rotation remains steady and orderly.

We need not despair during adversity: the wheel may turn in God's time.

Nor should prosperous people become proud, because their circumstances may quickly change.

The wheels stand beside the living creatures because angels serve in God's providential government.

The spirit of the living creatures is in the wheels.

The same divine wisdom, power and holiness that govern the angels direct events in the earthly world.

The wheel presents four faces, picturing Providence extending in every direction.

Wherever you look, there is a face of Providence turned toward you.

A wheel within a wheel expresses how complex and difficult to understand God's dealings can be.

Yet everything is wisely ordered.

The wheels move constantly and follow the Spirit without turning aside.

If we likewise followed the Spirit's direction, we would not repeatedly have to undo through repentance what we had done wrongly.

Their immense rims cause awe.

Thinking about the height and depth of God's counsel should humble us.

Their rims are full of eyes.

Every movement of Providence is directed by infinite wisdom.

The Lord's eyes see both good and evil everywhere.

There is no blind chance or fortune governing the world.

Above the creatures is a glorious yet fearsome firmament like crystal.

What seems to us a dark cloud is clear to God; he sees through it and knows all who live on earth.

When the angels have awakened a careless world, they lower their wings so that God's voice may be heard clearly.

The events of Providence should open our ears to God's revealed word.

The sounds of earth should lead us to listen to the voice from heaven.

How can we escape if we reject the One who speaks there?

The throne and the likeness of the Son of Man (verses 26–28)

Henry understands the figure on the throne as representing the eternal Son, the second Person of the Trinity, who would later assume human nature.

He first notices the throne.

It is a throne of glory, grace, triumph, government and judgment.

It is good news for humanity that the throne above the firmament is occupied by One who appears in the likeness of a human being.

A rainbow surrounds the throne.

This familiar sign of the covenant represents God's mercy and covenant love toward his people.

The fire of divine anger was about to break out against Jerusalem, yet limits would be set to the judgment.

God would remember his covenant.

Everything Ezekiel saw prepared him to hear what God would say.

When the prophet fell on his face, he heard the voice of One speaking.

God delights to teach the humble.

Therefore, let sinners humble themselves before him.

And let believers contemplate his glory so that the Spirit of the Lord may gradually transform them into his likeness.
classic_reading:
[Ezek.1.1-Ezek.1.14]
Ezekiel
Ezekiel was one of the priests; he was carried captive to Chaldea with Jehoiachin. All his prophecies appear to have been delivered in that country, at some place north of Babylon. Their chief object appears to have been to comfort his brethren in captivity. He is directed to warn of the dreadful calamities coming upon Judea, particularly upon the false prophets, and the neighbouring nations. Also to announce the future restoration of Israel and Judah from their several dispersions, and their happy state in their latter days, under the Messiah. Much of Christ will be found in this book, especially in the conclusion.
Chapter 1
Ezekiel's vision of God, and of the angelic host. ( [Ezek.1.1-Ezek.1.14] Ezek 1:1-14) The conduct of Divine Providence. ( [Ezek.1.15-Ezek.1.25] Ezek 1:15-25) A revelation of the Son of man upon his heavenly throne. ( [Ezek.1.26-Ezek.1.28] Ezek 1:26-28)
Verses 1-14 It is a mercy to have the word of God brought to us, and a duty to attend to it diligently, when we are in affliction. The voice of God came in the fulness of light and power, by the Holy Spirit. These visions seem to have been sent to possess the prophet's mind with great and high thoughts of God. To strike terror upon sinners. To speak comfort to those that feared God, and humbled themselves. In [Ezek.1.4-Ezek.1.14] Ezek 1:4-14, is the first part of the vision, which represents God as attended and served by a vast company of angels, who are all his messengers, his ministers, doing his commandments. This vision would impress the mind with solemn awe and fear of the Divine displeasure, yet raise expectations of blessings. The fire is surrounded with a glory. Though we cannot by searching find out God to perfection, yet we see the brightness round about it. The likeness of the living creatures came out of the midst of the fire; angels derive their being and power from God. They have the understanding of a man, and far more. A lion excels in strength and boldness. An ox excels in diligence and patience, and unwearied discharge of the work he has to do. An eagle excels in quickness and piercing sight, and in soaring high; and the angels, who excel man in all these respects, put on these appearances. The angels have wings; and whatever business God sends them upon, they lose no time. They stood straight, and firm, and steady. They had not only wings for motion, but hands for action. Many persons are quick, who are not active; they hurry about, but do nothing to purpose; they have wings, but no hands. But wherever the angels' wings carried them, they carried hands with them, to be doing what duty required. Whatever service they went about, they went every one straight forward. When we go straight, we go forward; when we serve God with one heart, we perform work. They turned not when they went. They made no mistakes; and their work needed not to be gone over again. They turned not from their business to trifle with any thing. They went whithersoever the Spirit of God would have them go. The prophet saw these living creatures by their own light, for their appearance was like burning coals of fire; they are seraphim, or "burners;" denoting the ardour of their love to God, and fervent zeal in his service. We may learn profitable lessons from subjects we cannot fully enter into or understand. But let us attend to the things which relate to our peace and duty, and leave secret things to the Lord, to whom alone they belong.
[Ezek.1.15-Ezek.1.25]
Verses 15-25 Providence, represented by the wheels, produces changes. Sometimes one spoke of the wheel is uppermost, sometimes another; but the motion of the wheel on its own axletree is regular and steady. We need not despond in adversity; the wheels are turning round and will raise us in due time, while those who presume in prosperity know not how soon they may be cast down. The wheel is near the living creatures; the angels are employed as ministers of God's providence. The spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels; the same wisdom, power, and holiness of God, that guide and govern the angels, by them order all events in this lower world. The wheel had four faces, denoting that the providence of God exerts itself in all parts. Look every way upon the wheel of providence, it has a face toward you. Their appearance and work were as a wheel in the middle of a wheel. The disposals of Providence seem to us dark, perplexed, and unaccountable, yet are all wisely ordered for the best. The motion of these wheels was steady, regular, and constant. They went as the Spirit directed, therefore returned not. We should not have to undo that by repentance which we have done amiss, if we followed the guidance of the Spirit. The rings, or rims of the wheels were so vast, that when put in motion the prophet was afraid to look upon them. The consideration of the height and depth of God's counsel should awe us. They were full of eyes round about. The motions of Providence are all directed by infinite Wisdom. All events are determined by the eyes of the Lord, which are in every place beholding the evil and the good; for there is no such thing as chance or fortune. The firmament above was a crystal, glorious, but terribly so. That which we take to be a dark cloud, is to God clear as crystal, through which he looks upon all the inhabitants of the earth. When the angels had roused a careless world, they let down their wings, that God's voice might be plainly heard. The voice of Providence is to open men's ears to the voice of the word. Sounds on earth should awaken our attention to the voice from heaven; for how shall we escape, if we turn away from Him that speaks from thence.
[Ezek.1.26-Ezek.1.28]
Verses 26-28 The eternal Son, the second Person in the Trinity, who afterwards took the human nature, is here denoted. The first thing observed was a throne. It is a throne of glory, a throne of grace, a throne of triumph, a throne of government, a throne of judgment. It is good news to men, that the throne above the firmament is filled with One who appears, even there, in the likeness of a man. The throne is surrounded with a rainbow, the well-known emblem of the covenant, representing God's mercy and covenanted love to his people. The fire of God's wrath was breaking out against Jerusalem, but bounds should be set to it; he would look upon the bow, and remember the covenant. All the prophet saw was only to prepare him for what he was to hear. When he fell on his face, he heard the voice of One that spake. God delights to teach the humble. Let sinners, then, humble themselves before him. And let believers think upon his glory, that they may be gradually changed into his image by the Spirit of the Lord.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe prophet is directed what he is to do.1–5And encouraged to be resolute, faithful, and devoted.6–10
Ezekiel is called to speak God's word (verses 1–5)

Ezekiel had received astonishing revelations.

To keep him from pride, God reminded him that he was still a son of man, a weak and mortal human being.

Yet the title could also be honorable, since Christ often called himself the Son of Man.

Ezekiel's prostrate posture showed reverence.

Standing upright would show greater readiness and fitness for his work.

God speaks to those who are prepared to do what he commands.

But Ezekiel lacked strength in himself.

The Spirit entered him and gave him the ability to stand.

God graciously works in us what he requires from us.

The Holy Spirit raises us to our feet by making our wills inclined toward duty.

When the Lord commands a sinner to awaken and attend to the soul's needs, the Spirit of life and grace accompanies that call.

Ezekiel was sent with God's message to the Israelites.

Many would despise it.

Yet the events would prove that a prophet had indeed been sent to them.

God's glory and the honor of his word will be upheld, whether the message becomes an aroma from life to life or from death to death.

Ezekiel must preach without fear (verses 6–10)

Anyone who wants to serve God effectively must not be ruled by fear of people.

The wicked are compared with briers and thorns, near to condemnation and burning.

The prophet must be faithful to the souls of those to whom he is sent.

Everyone who speaks God's message to others must first obey God's voice.

Discovering sin and hearing warnings of God's judgment should move us to grief and lamentation.

Those who understand God's word see that it contains terrible warnings for unrepentant sinners.

They also see that its precious gospel promises belong to repentant and believing servants of the Lord.
classic_reading:
[Ezek.2.1-Ezek.2.5]
Chapter 2
The prophet is directed what he is to do. ( [Ezek.2.1-Ezek.2.5] Ezek 2:1-5) And encouraged to be resolute, faithful, and devoted. ( [Ezek.2.6-Ezek.2.10] Ezek 2:6-10)
Verses 1-5 Lest Ezekiel should be lifted up with the abundance of the revelations, he is put in mind that still he is a son of man, a weak, mortal creature. As Christ usually called himself the Son of man, it was also an honourable distinction. Ezekiel's posture showed reverence, but his standing up would be a posture of greater readiness and fitness for business. God will speak to us, when we stand ready to do what he commands us. As Ezekiel had not strength of his own, the Spirit entered into him. God is graciously pleased to work in us whatever he requires of us. The Holy Spirit sets us upon our feet, by inclining our wills to our duty. Thus, when the Lord calls upon the sinner to awake, and attend to the concerns of his soul, the Spirit of life and grace comes with the call. Ezekiel is sent with a message to the children of Israel. Many might treat his message with contempt, yet they should know by the event that a prophet had been sent to them. God will be glorified, and his word made honourable, whether it be a savour of life unto life, or of death unto death.
[Ezek.2.6-Ezek.2.10]
Verses 6-10 Those who will do any thing to purpose in the service of God, must not fear men. Wicked men are as briers and thorns; but they are nigh unto cursing, and their end is to be burned. The prophet must be faithful to the souls of those to whom he was sent. All who speak from God to others, must obey his voice. The discoveries of sin, and the warnings of wrath, should be matter of lamentation. And those acquainted with the word of God, will clearly perceive it is filled with woe to impenitent sinners; and that all the precious promises of the gospel are for the repenting, believing servants of the Lord.

Original chapter outline — explicit verse-label correctionsOriginal outlineVersesThe preparation of the prophet for his work.1–11His office, as that of a watchman.12–21The restraining and restoring his speech.22–27
The prophet receives God's words (<reference osisRef="Ezek.3.1-Ezek.3.11" resp="BibleResourcesOriginalSourceRangeInModernSectionHeading">verses 1–11</reference>)

Ezekiel was to take God's truths into himself as food for his soul.

By feeding on them through faith, he would gain strength.

People changed by God's grace can receive with joy the same truths that bring terror to the wicked.

Ezekiel was to announce everything God had told him, and nothing beyond it.

How can anyone speak God's mind better than by using his words?

If people refused to listen, Ezekiel must not turn away in offense.

The people of Nineveh responded to Jonah's preaching, while Israel remained stubborn and unchanged.

We must leave such different outcomes under God's sovereignty and confess that his judgments are deep.

Those who refused the prophet's word also refused to learn from God's corrective judgments.

The Lord would strengthen Ezekiel.

He must continue earnestly preaching regardless of the immediate outcome.

Ezekiel is appointed a watchman (<reference osisRef="Ezek.3.12-Ezek.3.21" resp="BibleResourcesOriginalSourceRangeInModernSectionHeading">verses 12–21</reference>)

The prophet's mission caused holy angels to rejoice.

These events taught him that God had enough power to sustain him in his work.

Ezekiel was overwhelmed by grief over his people's sins and suffering, and by the majesty of the vision.

Solitude, reflection and fellowship with God can be precious.

Yet the Lord's servant must be prepared to serve the people of his generation.

God appointed Ezekiel to be a watchman for Israel.

If a watchman faithfully warns the wicked, he is not responsible for their refusal and ruin.

Although the passage concerns Israel's national covenant, Henry also applies its warning to the ultimate destiny of all people under every period of God's dealings.

Those who appear righteous need warnings as well as comfort.

Many become proud or careless, fall away and die in their sins.

Listeners to the gospel should welcome rebuke and warning, not only encouragement.

God regulates the prophet's speech (<reference osisRef="Ezek.3.22-Ezek.3.27" resp="BibleResourcesOriginalSourceRangeInModernSectionHeading">verses 22–27</reference>)

We owe every blessing of fellowship between God and humanity to Christ's mediation.

A genuine believer can say, “I am never less alone than when I am alone with God.”

When the Lord opened Ezekiel's mouth, the prophet was to speak boldly.

He must place life and death, blessing and curse, before the people, leaving them responsible for their response.
classic_reading:
[Ezek.3.1-Ezek.3.11]
Chapter 3
The preparation of the prophet for his work. ( [Ezek.3.1-Ezek.3.11] Ezek 3:1-11) His office, as that of a watchman. ( [Ezek.3.12-Ezek.3.21] Ezek 3:12-21) The restraining and restoring his speech. ( [Ezek.3.22-Ezek.3.27] Ezek 3:22-27)
Verses 1-11 Ezekiel was to receive the truths of God as the food for his soul, and to feed upon them by faith, and he would be strengthened. Gracious souls can receive those truths of God with delight, which speak terror to the wicked. He must speak all that, and that only, which God spake to him. How can we better speak God's mind than with his words? If disappointed as to his people, he must not be offended. The Ninevites were wrought upon by Jonah's preaching, when Israel was unhumbled and unreformed. We must leave this unto the Divine sovereignty, and say, Lord, thy judgments are a great deep. They will not regard the word of the prophet, for they will not regard the rod of God. Christ promises to strengthen him. He must continue earnest in preaching, whatever the success might be.
[Ezek.3.12-Ezek.3.21]
Verses 12-21 This mission made the holy angels rejoice. All this was to convince Ezekiel, that the God who sent him had power to bear him out in his work. He was overwhelmed with grief for the sins and miseries of his people, and overpowered by the glory of the vision he had seen. And however retirement, meditation, and communion with God may be sweet, the servant of the Lord must prepare to serve his generation. The Lord told the prophet he had appointed him a watchman to the house of Israel. If we warn the wicked, we are not chargeable with their ruin. Though such passages refer to the national covenant made with Israel, they are equally to be applied to the final state of all men under every dispensation. We are not only to encourage and comfort those who appear to be righteous, but they are to be warned, for many have grown high-minded and secure, have fallen, and even died in their sins. Surely then the hearers of the gospel should desire warnings, and even reproofs.
[Ezek.3.22-Ezek.3.27]
Verses 22-27 Let us own ourselves for ever indebted to the mediation of Christ, for the blessed intercourse between God and man; and a true believer will say, I am never less alone than when thus alone. When the Lord opened Ezekiel's mouth, he was to deliver his message boldly, to place life and death, the blessing and the curse, before the people, and leave them to their choice.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe siege of Jerusalem.1–8The famine the inhabitants would suffer.9–17
Ezekiel acts out Jerusalem's siege (verses 1–8)

The prophet was commanded to represent the siege of Jerusalem through signs.

He lay on his left side for a number of days, understood by Henry as possibly corresponding to the years since idolatry had become established.

The prophet's portrayal of the city's coming destruction served one purpose:

To show that sin was the cause provoking the ruin of a once-flourishing Jerusalem.

Ezekiel's restricted food pictures famine (verses 9–17)

The bread that sustained Ezekiel was to be made from coarse grains and legumes mixed together.

Such food was seldom used except during extreme scarcity.

Even that was to be eaten only in a small amount.

The sign represented the desperate shortage the Jews would suffer during the siege and captivity.

When Ezekiel objected, he did not say he had been raised delicately and had never endured hardship.

Instead, he appealed to his conscientious obedience to the law: he had never eaten food forbidden to him.

It will comfort us when hardship comes if our consciences testify that we have carefully avoided even the appearance of evil.

Consider the terrible ruin caused by sin and acknowledge that God's judgment is righteous.

The people had used abundance for luxury and excess.

Their punishment through famine corresponded to that misuse.

When people refuse to serve the Lord joyfully while they have everything they need, they may end up serving enemies while lacking even the necessities of life.
classic_reading:
[Ezek.4.1-Ezek.4.8]
Chapter 4
The siege of Jerusalem. ( [Ezek.4.1-Ezek.4.8] Ezek 4:1-8) The famine the inhabitants would suffer. ( [Ezek.4.9-Ezek.4.17] Ezek 4:9-17)
Verses 1-8 The prophet was to represent the siege of Jerusalem by signs. He was to lie on his left side for a number of days, supposed to be equal to the years from the establishment of idolatry. All that the prophet sets before the children of his people, about the destruction of Jerusalem, is to show that sin is the provoking cause of the ruin of that once flourishing city.
[Ezek.4.9-Ezek.4.17]
Verses 9-17 The bread which was Ezekiel's support, was to be made of coarse grain and pulse mixed together, seldom used except in times of urgent scarcity, and of this he was only to take a small quantity. Thus was figured the extremity to which the Jews were to be reduced during the siege and captivity. Ezekiel does not plead, Lord, from my youth I have been brought up delicately, and never used to any thing like this; but that he had been brought up conscientiously, and never had eaten any thing forbidden by the law. It will be comfortable when we are brought to suffer hardships, if our hearts can witness that we have always been careful to keep even from the appearance of evil. See what woful work sin makes, and acknowledge the righteousness of God herein. Their plenty having been abused to luxury and excess, they were justly punished by famine. When men serve not God with cheerfulness in the abundance of all things, God will make them serve their enemies in the want of all things.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesA type of hair, showing the judgments about to come upon the Jews.1–4These awful judgments are declared.5–17
The prophet's divided hair symbolizes the judgments (verses 1–4)

Ezekiel was commanded to shave his head and beard.

This signified God's complete rejection and abandonment of the people as they persisted in rebellion.

One portion of the hair would be burned inside the city, representing multitudes who would die from famine and disease.

Another would be cut apart, representing those killed by the sword.

A third would be scattered by the wind, representing people carried captive by the conqueror and others fleeing for safety to neighboring countries.

A small part of the scattered hair would be bound in the folds of his clothing to show how carefully a small remnant would be preserved.

Only a few people would be saved.

But sinners cannot escape God's anger merely by choosing a different hiding place.

The fire and sword of divine judgment will reach those who persist without repentance.

God announces the judgment upon Jerusalem (verses 5–17)

The sentence against Jerusalem is terrifying, and the language used makes it even more dreadful.

Who could stand before God when his anger is revealed?

Those who live and die without repentance face lasting judgment and will not be spared forever.

Neither people nor churches that change the Lord's commands should assume they will escape the judgment Jerusalem received.

Let us seek to honor the teaching of God our Savior in all we do.

Sooner or later, God's word will prove true.
classic_reading:
[Ezek.5.1-Ezek.5.4]
Chapter 5
A type of hair, showing the judgments about to come upon the Jews. ( [Ezek.5.1-Ezek.5.4] Ezek 5:1-4) These awful judgments are declared. ( [Ezek.5.5-Ezek.5.17] Ezek 5:5-17)
Verses 1-4 The prophet must shave off the hair of his head and beard, which signifies God's utter rejecting and abandoning that people. One part must be burned in the midst of the city, denoting the multitudes that should perish by famine and pestilence. Another part was to be cut in pieces, representing the many who were slain by the sword. Another part was to be scattered in the wind, denoting the carrying away of some into the land of the conqueror, and the flight of others into the neighbouring countries for shelter. A small quantity of the third portion was to be bound in his shirts, as that of which he is very careful. But few were reserved. To whatever refuge sinners flee, the fire and sword of God's wrath will consume them.
[Ezek.5.5-Ezek.5.17]
Verses 5-17 The sentence passed upon Jerusalem is very dreadful, the manner of expression makes it still more so. Who is able to stand in God's sight when he is angry? Those who live and die impenitent, will perish for ever unpitied; there is a day coming when the Lord will not spare. Let not persons or churches, who change the Lord's statutes, expect to escape the doom of Jerusalem. Let us endeavour to adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in all things. Sooner or later God's word will prove itself true.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe Divine judgments for idolatry.1–7A remnant shall be saved.8–10The calamities are to be lamented.11–14
Idolatry brings God's judgments (verses 1–7)

War lays waste to people, places and even things that are regarded as most sacred.

God can destroy idolatry through the hands of idolaters themselves.

He is right to turn into a desolation anything we have made an idol.

Superstitions upon which people rely for safety often become the cause of their destruction.

Henry looks forward to a day when idols and idolatry will be removed from the professedly Christian church as thoroughly as they were eventually removed from among the Jews.

A small remnant will be preserved (verses 8–10)

A remnant of Israel would survive.

In time these people would remember the Lord, their obligations to him and their earlier rebellion.

Those who sincerely repent recognize sin as the hateful thing God abhors.

They become deeply ashamed of themselves because of the sins they committed.

Their repentance brings glory to God.

Whatever awakens us to remember him and to recognize the wrong we have done against him should be received as a blessing.

Lamentation and compassion for sinners (verses 11–14)

Our duty is not only to grieve over our own sin and suffering.

We should also have compassion for the misery that other people bring upon themselves through wickedness.

Sin devastates.

Therefore stand in awe of God and turn away from it.

If we appreciate the worth of human souls and the danger facing those who do not believe, we will consider the salvation of even one sinner who flees to Jesus an ample reward for all the contempt or opposition we may encounter in serving him.
classic_reading:
[Ezek.6.1-Ezek.6.7]
Chapter 6
The Divine judgments for idolatry. ( [Ezek.6.1-Ezek.6.7] Ezek 6:1-7) A remnant shall be saved. ( [Ezek.6.8-Ezek.6.10] Ezek 6:8-10) The calamities are to be lamented. ( [Ezek.6.11-Ezek.6.14] Ezek 6:11-14)
Verses 1-7 . War desolates persons, places, and things esteemed most sacred. God ruins idolatries even by the hands of idolaters. It is just with God to make that a desolation, which we make an idol. The superstitions to which many trust for safety, often cause their ruin. And the day is at hand, when idols and idolatry will be as thoroughly destroyed from the professedly Christian church as they were from among the Jews.
[Ezek.6.8-Ezek.6.10]
Verses 8-10 A remnant of Israel should be left; at length they should remember the Lord, their obligations to him, and rebellion against him. True penitents see sin to be that abominable thing which the Lord hates. Those who truly loathe sin, loathe themselves because of sin. They give glory to God by their repentance. Whatever brings men to remember Him, and their sins against him, should be regarded as a blessing.
[Ezek.6.11-Ezek.6.14]
Verses 11-14 It is our duty to be affected, not only with our own sins and sufferings, but to look with compassion upon the miseries wicked people bring upon themselves. Sin is a desolating thing; therefore, stand in awe, and sin not. If we know the worth of souls, and the danger to which unbelievers are exposed, we shall deem every sinner who takes refuge in Jesus from the wrath to come, an abundant recompence for all contempt or opposition we may meet with.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe desolation of the land.1–15The distress of the few who should escape.16–22The captivity.23–27
The end of the land's prosperity (verses 1–15)

The abruptness and repetition of this prophecy show how deeply the prophet was moved by the disaster he foresaw.

The final destruction of unrepentant sinners will be just as inescapable.

Oh, may the wicked person's wrongdoing come to an end before it brings the person to an end!

For someone who refuses repentance, trouble does nothing but harm: it hardens the heart and stirs sinful desires.

Yet God can, through his grace, make the very same suffering a means of much good for another person.

The day of genuine trouble was near—not merely rumors or distant echoes.

Whatever visible effects God's judgment produces, our sin is the root beneath them.

The judgments would spread everywhere.

God would be glorified in all of them.

Now is the time of the Lord's patience and mercy.

But the time when sinners face judgment is approaching.

The surviving people suffer (verses 16–22)

Sooner or later sin brings sorrow.

Those who will not repent may justly be left to waste away under the sins they refuse to abandon.

For many people, wealth is a snare leading to ruin.

Gaining the whole world can mean losing the soul.

Riches do not help in the day of God's anger.

The world's possessions cannot meet the soul's deepest needs or bring lasting satisfaction in distress.

Even God's temple would be no protection for people who rejected his ways.

Those unwilling to be ruled by the power of godliness are unworthy to keep the honor of its outward form.

God's judgment brings captivity (verses 23–27)

People who break free of the obligations of God's law will find themselves bound by the chains of his judgment.

Because they encouraged one another in sin, the Lord would cause them to lose courage.

When God judges people according to what they deserve, distress reaches everyone.

May he enable us to seek the good portion that can never be taken away.

The idolatry within the temple (verses 1–6)

In a vision, the glorious figure Ezekiel saw seemed to take hold of him and carry him in the Spirit to Jerusalem.

There he saw a place prepared for a degrading idol within the inner court of the temple.

The entire scene was presented to the prophet as a vision.

If God gave any of us a clear view of his glory and majesty alongside the many abominations practiced in a city, we would see the justice of even his severest judgments against that city.

The elders' secret worship (verses 7–12)

A hidden room was opened to Ezekiel.

The walls were covered with pictures of creatures, and elders of Israel worshiped before them.

High position in the world does not preserve people from sinful desires or idolatry if they are abandoned to the deceit of their own hearts.

Some who quickly tire of God's service are willing to spend great time, labor and money on superstition.

Hypocrites try to conceal themselves behind a wall of outward profession.

Yet some opening remains through which careful observers may discover what they are really doing.

Much wickedness is practiced in secret.

These people imagined God could not see them.

Those who try to make the Lord responsible for their sins are especially ready for judgment.

Tammuz, sun worship and the depth of corruption (verses 13–18)

The annual mourning for Tammuz was associated, in Henry's account, with shameful practices.

He supposes that those worshiping the sun were priests.

The Lord called Ezekiel to recognize the gravity of these sins.

The reference to putting a branch to the nose is, in Henry's explanation, a custom performed in honor of an idol.

The more closely we examine human nature and our own hearts, the more wrongdoing we discover.

The more earnestly a believer searches the heart, the more humbly that person should stand before God and the more highly value the fountain opened for cleansing from sin.

Let us seek to wash there.

If it should please God to give any man a clear view of his glory and majesty, and of all the abominations committing in any one city, he would then admit the justice of the severest punishments God should inflict thereon.

No superiority in worldly matters will preserve men from lust, or idolatries, when they are left to their own deceitful hearts; and those who are soon wearied in the service of God, often grudge no toil nor expense when following their superstitions. When hypocrites screen themselves behind the wall of an outward profession, there is some hole or other left in the wall, something that betrays them to those who look diligently. [Ezek.8.13-Ezek.8.18]
Verses 13-18 The yearly lamenting for Tammuz was attended with infamous practices; and the worshippers of the sun here described, are supposed to have been priests. The more we examine human nature and our own hearts, the more abominations we shall discover; and the longer the believer searches himself, the more he will humble himself before God, and the more will he value the fountain open for sin, and seek to wash therein.

Original heading

A vision denoting the destruction of the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and the departure of the symbol of the Divine presence.

The faithful remnant is marked (verses 1–4)

It is a great comfort for believers that, even among destroyers and destruction, there is a Mediator.

He is the great High Priest, with access to heaven, and believers on earth have an interest in him.

God's glory appeared to move from above the ark toward the threshold.

This signified that the Lord was about to leave his mercy seat and announce judgment against the people.

Those marked for preservation were known by their sorrow over Jerusalem's sins.

They sighed and cried to God in prayer because of the abominations taking place in the city.

Those whom God keeps pure amid widespread wickedness he can keep safe amid widespread distress.

The judgment begins at the sanctuary (verses 5–11)

The slaughter was to begin in the sanctuary.

This showed that God is especially displeased by sins committed by people nearest to him and most privileged by his gifts.

The person appointed to protect the faithful reported that his task was completed.

This points, in Henry's application, to Christ's perfect faithfulness to his Father's trust.

The Son was appointed to give eternal life to the people entrusted to him.

He declares that he has lost none whom the Father gave him.

If we are rescued while others perish, all the credit belongs to God's mercy.

We too have deserved his wrath.

We should continue interceding for others.

But wherever the Lord shows judgment rather than mercy, he acts with no injustice: he gives people what their ways deserve.
classic_reading:
[Ezek.9.1-Ezek.9.4]
Chapter 9
A vision denoting the destruction of the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and the departure of the symbol of the Divine presence.
Verses 1-4 It is a great comfort to believers, that in the midst of destroyers and destructions, there is a Mediator, a great High Priest, who has an interest in heaven, and in whom saints on earth have an interest. The representation of the Divine glory from above the ark, removed to the threshold, denoted that the Lord was about to leave his mercy-seat, and to pronounce judgment on the people. The distinguishing character of this remnant that is to be saved, is such as sigh and cry to God in prayer, because of the abominations in Jerusalem. Those who keep pure in times of general wickedness, God will keep safe in times of general trouble and distress.
[Ezek.9.5-Ezek.9.11]
Verses 5-11 The slaughter must begin at the sanctuary, that all may see and know that the Lord hates sin most in those nearest to him. He who was appointed to protect, reported the matter. Christ is faithful to the trust reposed in him. Is he commanded by his Father to secure eternal life to the chosen remnant? He says, Of all that thou hast given me, I have lost none. If others perish, and we are saved, we must ascribe the difference wholly to the mercy of our God, for we too have deserved wrath. Let us still continue to plead in behalf of others. But where the Lord shows no mercy he does no injustice; he only recompenses men's ways.

Fire from among the cherubim (verses 1–7)

The fire taken from between the wheels, beneath the cherubim, recalls Ezekiel 1:13.

Henry understands it as a sign of God's anger about to fall upon Jerusalem.

The vision shows that divine judgment is not arbitrary.

The fire of God's wrath, which brings judgment upon a nation, is just and holy.

It also points toward the great day when the earth and all its works will be consumed.

The glory of the Lord departs (verses 8–22)

Ezekiel saw how divine Providence governs events in the world.

When God withdraws from a people who have provoked his displeasure, angels above and events on earth serve to accomplish his purpose.

The Spirit of life, the Spirit of God, directs every creature in heaven and on earth so that each contributes to the divine plan.

God's departure from a rebellious people takes place by degrees.

Even when the Lord is ready to leave, he would return if the people repented and prayed.

May this warn sinners to seek the Lord while he may be found and call upon him while he is near.

And may it cause us all to walk humbly and carefully with our God.

[Ezek.10.8-Ezek.10.22]
Verses 8-22 Ezekiel sees the working of Divine providence in the government of the lower world, and the affairs of it. When God is leaving a people in displeasure, angels above, and all events below, further his departure. The Spirit of life, the Spirit of God, directs all creatures, in heaven and on earth, so as to make them serve the Divine purpose. God removes by degrees from a provoking people; and, when ready to depart, would return to them, if they were a repenting, praying people. Let this warn sinners to seek the Lord while he may be found, and to call on him while he is near, and cause us all to walk humbly and watchfully with our God.
